clue.text: Film on revolutionary Lavoisier, perhaps?

indicators.note: in an across clue 'on' places the film piece after the revolutionary

parts.note: Che Guevara is the crossword's stock revolutionary
a film is a thin layer or haze, a mist on glass

explanation.surface: Someone proposes a movie about a revolutionary French scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary Lavoisier' reads as one person, but the revolutionary is Che and Lavoisier, a pioneering eighteenth-century scientist, is the example that the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: Antoine Lavoisier, father of modern chemistry, is an example of a scientist working with chemical elements.

clue.text: Hold cups up in time

indicators.note: the reversed garment goes inside the time word

parts.note: an hour is a measure of time

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a bra has cups

explanation.surface: Cups are held raised in time, like a toast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns BRA into ARB, which goes inside HOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep or harbour a grudge is to hold it, a verb sense.

clue.text: In the end, nut goes in to secure wheels

indicators.note: that letter is put inside the securing word

parts.note: to secure a boat is to moor it

indicators.note: the end of the word nut is its last letter

explanation.surface: A mechanic's job: the last nut goes on to fasten the wheels.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheels is slang for a car, a vehicle you drive.

clue.text: Model upset by small group with their own characteristics

definitions.text: small group with their own characteristics

indicators.note: to model is to shape or mould, so the letters of the following words are reshaped

explanation.surface: A fashion model is thrown by a clique with quirks all their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like the definition, a type, but it is the verb: it reworks the letters of 'upset by'. 'upset' also tempts as the indicator, yet it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A subdivision within a category whose members share distinguishing traits.

clue.text: London gardens, grass borders taking an oblique course

indicators.note: the informer's word is set on both sides of the gardens, bordering them

parts.note: to grass is to inform, to sing to the police
Kew Gardens, the botanic gardens in south-west London

explanation.surface: The edging of lawns at a famous London garden runs off at a slant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass borders' looks like turf edging, but grass is the verb meaning to inform (SING) and 'borders' wraps it round KEW, the botanic gardens in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Veering at a slant is moving off-line, going on an oblique path.

clue.text: See 24
Trojan king captured by Greek character with less fine clothing

indicators.note: the comparative word clothes, wraps around, the rest

parts.note: less fine means worse

indicators.note: the king's letter is taken inside the Greek letter

parts.note: rho is a letter of the Greek alphabet
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A Trojan king is taken prisoner by a Greek, dressed in shabbier clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trojan' tempts with Troy's King Priam, but it is the definition: one who works like a Trojan. K goes inside RHO, and WORSE clothes the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who works like a Trojan is a tireless, dependable labourer.

clue.text: Nationalist movement primarily welcoming extreme characters, one is — describing this?

definitions.text: Nationalist movement primarily welcoming extreme characters, one is — describing this?

indicators.note: the two first letters take in the rest between them
primarily picks the first letters of the two words

parts.note: A and Z are the extreme characters of the alphabet
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A nationalist movement that welcomed extremists: which one is being described?
explanation.walkthrough: N and M (first letters of 'Nationalist movement') welcome AZ, I and IS; the whole clue also describes the ideology.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitler's party was a nationalist movement that drew in extremists, so the clue defines its ideology.

clue.text: Luddite, one with job in peril, surprisingly flexible?

indicators.note: in peril means threatened, unsettled, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A machine-hater whose job is at risk proves unexpectedly adaptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in peril' signals the anagram of LUDDITE, ONE and JOB; a Luddite opposed new machinery that threatened jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Having unusually supple joints, able to bend limbs in surprising ways.

clue.text: Having wiped back, beast is dry

indicators.note: wiping the back end off the word for the beast removes its last letter

parts.note: a beast is a savage creature, a BRUTE

explanation.surface: After rubbing down its rear, an animal is left dry.
explanation.definitionFit: The French wine term for champagne with very little sugar, the driest style.

clue.text: Alongside particular short, drink bottles as reward for failure

indicators.note: the drink word contains the rest, as a bottle holds liquid

parts.note: booze is alcoholic drink
by means beside, alongside

indicators.note: short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: particular in the sense of fussy, prim

explanation.surface: Someone fussy, a little drunk, takes home a bottle as a consolation award.
explanation.walkthrough: PRIM (particular, fussy) cut short gives PRI; BY and PRI together go inside BOOZE, which 'bottles' them.
explanation.definitionFit: A joke award given to the competitor who comes last.

clue.text: Joyful cry that may be 9?

parts.note: the cheer comes after 'hip hip', two hips, and so is cheekily called double-jointed, the answer to 9

explanation.surface: A cry of joy described as though it had extra-bendy joints.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is DOUBLE-JOINTED: the cheer traditionally follows 'hip hip', so it comes with two hip joints.
explanation.definitionFit: A shout of delight or triumph, the third word of the traditional three cheers.

clue.text: Hard caught up in it, lie with men and bloody head wound in battle

indicators.note: the hard letter is caught up inside the jumble that follows, 'it'
the head of the word bloody is its first letter
wound as in twisted round, so these letters are wound into a new order

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A grim battlefield scene: lying with other men, a bleeding head wound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound' reads as an injury but is the past tense of wind, giving BLENEIM from LIE, MEN and B; H is 'caught up in it'.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1704 victory of Marlborough over the French in Bavaria, a famous battle.

clue.text: Assorted receipts, about fifty for drink

indicators.note: the mixed letters go round the numeral, about it
assorted means mixed up, so the letters of receipts are mixed

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A pile of mixed receipts, around fifty of them, for drinks bought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assorted' scrambles RECEIPTS, which then goes 'about' L, the Roman fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: An orange-flavoured liqueur, a drink served in cocktails.

clue.text: Material girls in conversation?

indicators.note: in conversation means as spoken, so the names are heard rather than written

parts.note: two girls' names, Polly and Esther

explanation.surface: Girls chatting about some material.
explanation.definitionFit: A synthetic fabric used for clothing, a material.

clue.text: See 22
See 27
Elizabeth I's favourite beer in curtailed privilege

indicators.note: the beer goes inside the shortened word
curtailed means cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a right is a privilege
ale is beer

explanation.surface: The Queen's favourite tipple: beer served as a limited privilege.
explanation.walkthrough: 'favourite' suggests a drink, but it means a royal favourite, a courtier.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter, the explorer and courtier, was a favourite of Queen Elizabeth I.

clue.text: One entering contracted agreement, gate's opening and closing for doorkeeper

indicators.note: the numeral goes into the shortened word
contracted means shortened, losing its last letter

parts.note: acting in concert means acting in agreement
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the opening and closing letters of the word gate

explanation.surface: Someone joins a short-term deal for a gate that opens and shuts, a porter's job.
explanation.walkthrough: CONCERT (agreement) contracted is CONCER; I enters it, then G and E, the first and last of 'gate', follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel or apartment porter who keeps the door and helps guests.

clue.text: For every income, a host

parts.note: per means for every, and income splits as in come: read together they say per goes in come

explanation.surface: A host's earnings, counted per event.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue word 'income' does two jobs at once: split as 'in come', its first half signals containment and its second half is the container for PER, Latin for 'for every'.
explanation.definitionFit: A master of ceremonies who hosts a show and introduces the acts.

clue.text: Over-eighteen set to drink wine regularly

indicators.note: the group word drinks, takes in, those letters

parts.note: a set is a group

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of wine

explanation.surface: Someone now an adult, ready to drink wine regularly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone over eighteen is legally an adult.

clue.text: Tycoon requiring a wig, lacking leadership: a word of caution about this arse

indicators.note: the warning word goes round the trimmed word

parts.note: a cautionary 'don't!'

indicators.note: lacking its first letter, its leader

parts.note: someone needing a wig is bald
the arse is the rump, the backside

explanation.surface: A rude jibe at a wig-wearing property tycoon.
explanation.walkthrough: BALD (requiring a wig) loses B; DONT goes about ALD, then RUMP follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The US property tycoon of the 2010s, famous for his hair, later president.

clue.text: Rare moment related to rare occurrence

parts.note: a blue steak is cooked very rare
MO is short for a moment, as in 'half a mo'
on means about, related to

explanation.surface: A rare instant connected to something that hardly ever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'rare's do different jobs: the first is meat barely cooked (BLUE), the second is part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: From the idiom 'once in a', meaning something that happens very seldom.

clue.text: In horror, one left disheartened by unfinished home in new town

indicators.note: in the horror means placed inside the word for it

parts.note: a little horror is a mischievous child, a monkey
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: losing its heart, the word left drops its middle letters

parts.note: the word left in full

indicators.note: an unfinished word stops short, so the bird's home loses its final letter

parts.note: a bird's home is its nest

explanation.surface: A frightening scene: someone dispirited after a half-built house in a new town.
explanation.walkthrough: LEFT disheartened loses EF to give LT; I and LT go inside MONKEY, and NEST unfinished gives NES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Buckinghamshire town built in the late 1960s as one of Britain's planned new towns.

clue.text: Finally, ball is placed on spot (but not the centre) for scorer

indicators.note: finally points to what comes at the very end, the closing letter of ball
the middle letter of the spot word is removed

parts.note: a zit is a pimple, a spot

explanation.surface: A football scene: the ball is placed on the penalty spot, off-centre, for the striker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scorer' is no goalscorer but a composer who scores music. ZIT loses its centre I to give ZT.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz, the Hungarian Romantic composer, wrote musical scores.

clue.text: Asian film stars in contest

indicators.note: the film and stars go inside the contest word

parts.note: to vie is to contest, compete
E.T. is the Spielberg film
stars are big names

explanation.surface: An Asian movie whose leading actors compete in a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from the South-East Asian country with Hanoi as its capital is an Asian.

clue.text: Duty beyond member in retirement, not having kids

indicators.note: the duty comes beyond, after, the reversed member
retiring means going back, so the word for the member is read backwards

parts.note: the male member
a duty is one's role

explanation.surface: A retired member of some body, with duties done and no children.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul's trademark smut: 'member' is the body part, reversed to SINEP. The answer is Latin legal phrase meaning without offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin legal term means without issue, used of someone who died childless.

clue.text: Sham, as boxer punched by Bill after beginning of count

indicators.note: the animal with its advert comes after the count's first letter
the first letter of the word count
the advert piece goes into the animal, punching through it

parts.note: hares famously box in spring, so a hare is a boxer
AD is short for advertisement, a bill

explanation.surface: A fake fight: a boxer hit by someone named Bill after the referee starts counting.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxer is no fighter but a HARE, since hares box; AD goes inside it after C.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretence or farce, an absurd show put on to deceive.

clue.text: Try to conceal evidence at first, with criminal past in state police

indicators.note: the try word conceals the rest within it

parts.note: to have a go is to try

indicators.note: the first letter of evidence
criminal suggests the letters of past are corrupted, rearranged

explanation.surface: Dodgy police try to hide evidence of a criminal past.
explanation.walkthrough: E (evidence at first) and STAP ('criminal' rearranging PAST) are concealed by GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The secret police force of Nazi Germany, an organ of the state.
